newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian budget - Bonds look for budget benefits.
newsitem.headline: Australian budget - Bonds look for budget benefits.

text.p: Next Tuesday's 1997/98 Australian federal budget is expected to be a largely consolidative affair after the government's aggressive fiscal stance last year.

However, bond market analysts are anticipating some positive surprises, which could see 10-year bond yields have one last fling down to 7.50 percent before the market builds in the growth story and tighter monetary policy further down the track.
Three positive outcomes are for an early balanced underlying budget, little or no fixed-interest rate bond supply, and, as a reward for fiscal restraint, a credit rating upgrade.
While the final say on the latter is out of the government's hands, another solid budget could help towards raising Australia's international standing on global debt markets.
"Our call is that there is a 70 percent probablity that we'll get an upgrade in the next 12 months," said Citibank chief economist Stephen Koukoulas.
However, Koukoulas' believes that the credit rating agencies would want to see how the current account fairs during a period of slightly stronger growth.
Standard & Poor's revised Australia's long-term foreign currency AA rating outlook to postive after the last budget.
At the time, S&P said that an upgrade of the rating would be dependent on the maintenance of a tight fiscal policy stance.
Analysts are also expecting another cut in the funding task for 1997/98, which could see little or no fixed-income bond issuance by the Treasury on a headline budget surplus approaching A$10 billion.

Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) estimates that based on a headline budget surplus of A$9.7 billion there will be a funding task of A$2.7 billion, taking into account A$7.5 billion of fixed-interest bond maturities and A$3.7 billion of Treasury adjustable rate bonds (TABS) expiring in 1997/98.

"The total financing task appears set to fall to around A$2.7 billion. This would be a little over half that expected for 1996/97 and well down on the A$20 billion outcome recorded in 1993/94 and 1994/95," CBA economists said a budget preview.
"With the financing task falling short of bond maturities, the stock of Commonwealth Government securities should decline over the next couple of years," the report added.
Citibank is assuming a A$10 billion headline surplus which would bring the net finance requirement close to zero.
"There may be a bit of shuffling of the yield curve, they might want to issue a new long bond and buy back some illiquid stock, but in net terms it's going to be zero," Citibank's Koukoulas said.

Looking further ahead, Deutsche Morgan Greenfell expects budget surpluses and large asset sales receipts implying a net retirement of bonds in each of the next four years, which will result in a serious reduction in market liquidity.
They estimate an overall contraction in the market from A$83 billion at June 30, 1997 to some A$66 billion at June 30, 2001.

"Such an eventuality, at a time of growing pension funds under management should promote the further development of the Australian corporate bond market and increased demand for mortgage-backed issues and other securitised receivables," said Ivan Colhoun, associate director at Deutsche.

A recent Reuters poll of 20 economists found the median forecast centring on a underlying budget deficit starting point for 1997/98 at A$3.8 billion and a target of A$2.1 billion deficit for the fiscal year. However, two economists expect the budget to be balanced a year than the government's projection.
